"There is, these days, a commonly held presumption in favor of knowledge, truth, and the uncovering and dissemination of information. It is rare to find somebody who self-identifies as an obscurantist or who openly espouses obscurantism as a legitimate policy instrument of wide utility.

Although nobody makes a brief for ignorance generally, there are many special cases in which ignorance is cultivated—in order, for example, to protect national security, sexual innocence, jury impartiality; to preserve anonymity for patients, clients, reviewers, and voters; to create suspense in films and novels; to protect trade secrets; to measure the placebo effect and avoid various research biases; and to create mental challenges for gaming and study. These cases are commonly accepted exceptions to the general rule of knowledge-favoring."

- Nick Bostrom, Information Hazards: A Typology of Potential Harms from Knowledge, published 2011

This website explores the typology of information hazards, and how, where, and why they manifest. Structured based on Nick Bostrom's writing on information hazards, it is divided into 6 main categories, with subtypes and examples for each. Note that due to the nature of infohazards, warnings may be included on certain entries that may cause distress to the viewer.
